lessons.title: Yield the small pieces, assemble the product
explanation: The yield model said a large die loses to the same defect density. Chiplets are the arithmetic response: cut the product into smaller dice that yield, then assemble them. Each chiplet sees a smaller A in e^(−A·D). The product's area comes back at packaging time, where a bond fail is a different class than a stochastic via on a 400 mm² monolith.

What you spend is an interconnect that used to be on-die: latency, energy, and a thermal and mechanical interface. What you buy is yield, mix-and-match process nodes, and the right to bin or replace a piece. A chiplet strategy that ignores the yield model is a marketing deck. A yield model that ignores the assembly fail rate is also incomplete.
Read 'chiplets improve yield' as: smaller A, then a new factory after the fab. Advanced packaging, next, is that factory.
lessons.example: A 400 mm² GPU-class die yields poorly. Four 100 mm² chiplets on the same front-end yield. Assembly loses a few percent to bond and known-good-die test. The product still ships more good systems than the monolith did.
lessons.whyItMatters: If chiplets are fashion, hybrid bonding will look like glue. If they are e^(−A·D) plus an assembly yield, you know which number to ask for.

quiz.stem: Chiplets yield small die and assemble the product because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Each piece sees a smaller area in the yield model, and the product is rebuilt after the fab

distractors.text: Defect density automatically falls when you saw the wafer
distractors.rationale: D did not change. A did.

distractors.text: k1 is the number of chiplets
distractors.rationale: k1 is lithography.

distractors.text: Assembly deletes the need for a yield model
distractors.rationale: Assembly has its own fail rate.

quiz.correctExplanation: Smaller A, then a new join. That is the move.
objectiveIds: Explain chiplets as yielding small die and assembling the product

quiz.stem: A monolith that dies where four smaller dice on the same flow live usually hit:
quiz.correctAnswer: The area term in the yield model, not a new species of defect that only hates large rectangles

distractors.text: A High-NA field that cannot cover a large die at all
distractors.rationale: Fields stitch. Area is the yield term here.

distractors.text: Poisson being repealed for small dice only
distractors.rationale: The same law makes the large one worse.

distractors.text: A pellicle that only fits small die
distractors.rationale: A membrane is not this area law.

quiz.correctExplanation: Same D, bigger A, worse Y. Cutting A is the chiplet bet.
objectiveIds: Predict why a large monolithic die loses to the same defect density

quiz.stem: Chiplets versus one monolith is a trade because:
quiz.correctAnswer: You buy yield and mix-and-match, and you spend an interconnect, a thermal interface, and assembly yield

distractors.text: Assembly is always lossless and free
distractors.rationale: Bonds fail. Tests cost.

distractors.text: Smaller dice automatically have infinite overlay margin
distractors.rationale: On-die overlay did not vanish.

distractors.text: Cutting a die repeals stochastic EUV defects
distractors.rationale: Each chiplet still prints its own vias.

quiz.correctExplanation: e^(−A·D) versus a new join. Both numbers have to win.
objectiveIds: Predict why a large monolithic die loses to the same defect density

lessons.title: Memory cubes next to compute, with a thermal bill
explanation: HBM is a chiplet story specialized to memory: stacked DRAM dice, a logic base, a short, wide interconnect sitting next to compute. Bandwidth per watt and per millimetre of edge look brilliant because the wires are short and many. The cube is also a heater sitting on the same package as a heater.

What it does not repeal: DRAM refresh and retention physics, the thermal resistance of the stack, and the mechanical stress of many bonds in a tall cube. A system that 'adds HBM' and then throttles in a sustained load hit the thermal bill, not a surprise about capacity.
Read HBM as chiplets plus a thermal interface, not as a magic memory type. Advanced packaging is how the cube is actually joined.
lessons.example: A package with a compute die and an HBM cube hits the advertised bandwidth in a burst and then clocks down. The cube's top dice are hot. The interconnect did its job. The heat path did not.
lessons.whyItMatters: If HBM is only a bandwidth slogan, you will misread every 'we attached a cube' announcement. The missing noun is usually heat.

quiz.stem: HBM is memory cubes next to compute because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Stacked DRAM with a short, wide join buys bandwidth; the cube still sits on the same package thermal budget

distractors.text: The stack deletes the need for DRAM refresh
distractors.rationale: Retention physics did not leave.

distractors.text: k1 is the number of DRAM dice
distractors.rationale: k1 is lithography.

distractors.text: The cube runs without any interconnect
distractors.rationale: The join is the product.

quiz.correctExplanation: Short wires, many of them, next to a heater. That is HBM.
objectiveIds: Describe HBM as memory cubes next to compute, with a thermal bill

quiz.stem: A package that makes the burst bandwidth and then throttles usually hit:
quiz.correctAnswer: The stack's thermal path, not a sudden loss of the interconnect's wire count

distractors.text: Poisson deleting every other DRAM bit
distractors.rationale: A thermal throttle is not a yield model.

distractors.text: The High-NA stitch on the cube
distractors.rationale: This is a package thermal, not a field seam.

distractors.text: A wet oxide grown in the TSVs during burst
distractors.rationale: No oxidant step ran in the benchmark.

quiz.correctExplanation: The wires worked. The heat did not leave. That is the bill.
objectiveIds: Predict a thermal or interconnect limit that the stack does not repeal

quiz.stem: More HBM stacks versus a hotter, closer cube is a trade because:
quiz.correctAnswer: More cubes buy bandwidth and spend package area and more thermal interfaces; closer spends heat into the compute die

distractors.text: Stacking always cools the compute die
distractors.rationale: A cube is a heater.

distractors.text: Bandwidth deletes the thermal resistance of the join
distractors.rationale: Short wires still sit in a stack of dice.

distractors.text: HBM stacking repeals DRAM retention physics at the cell
distractors.rationale: The physics of the cell remains.

quiz.correctExplanation: Wires versus heat. The cube does not let you pick both for free.
objectiveIds: Predict a thermal or interconnect limit that the stack does not repeal

lessons.title: The factory after the fab
explanation: Once the product is several dice, someone has to join them. Advanced packaging is that factory: organic substrates, silicon interposers, silicon bridges, and hybrid bonds that join copper pad to copper pad at pitches solder cannot. Hybrid bonding is how 'chiplet density' becomes a real number rather than a slide. A solder bump is a fat, forgiving, thermally mediocre join. A hybrid bond is a dense, unforgiving, thermally better join.

The bill is cleanliness, overlay of die-to-die marks, and a known-good-die test that has to be right before you spend the bond. A particle that was a nuisance on a bump is a killer on a hybrid pad. You have seen that sentence at wafer CD. It recurs here.
Read 'hybrid bonding improves chiplet density' as: the join pitch shrank, so the pad is now a leading-edge overlay and defectivity problem on a package tool.
lessons.example: A solder-bumped interposer cannot fit the wire count a compute-HBM pair wants. A hybrid-bonded pair can. A single particle on a pad, invisible at bump scale, opens the pair. The clean that used to be 'good enough' for bumps is now the yield model.
lessons.whyItMatters: If packaging is 'assembly', you will miss that the join inherited lithography's overlay and defectivity budgets. The factory moved; the physics did not retire.

quiz.stem: Advanced packaging is the factory after the fab because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Interposers, bridges, and hybrid bonds join yielded dice into the product the wafer no longer is

distractors.text: Packaging replaces lithography and front-end entirely
distractors.rationale: The dice still have to be made.

distractors.text: k1 is defined as the bump pitch of the hybrid bond pad
distractors.rationale: k1 is wafer lithography.

distractors.text: Solder automatically becomes a Bragg mirror
distractors.rationale: A bump is a join, not an EUV optic.

quiz.correctExplanation: Yield the pieces, then a second factory joins them. That is the course's last module.
objectiveIds: Describe advanced packaging as interposers, bridges, and hybrid bonds after the fab

quiz.stem: A hybrid-bond open that a solder bump of the same net would have survived is usually:
quiz.correctAnswer: A particle or overlay miss at a pad pitch solder never had to hit

distractors.text: Proof that copper cannot be a conductor
distractors.rationale: The pad is copper. It missed.

distractors.text: A High-NA stitch on the organic substrate only
distractors.rationale: This is die-to-die pad overlay.

distractors.text: Wet oxidation of the compute ISA
distractors.rationale: No architecture melted.

quiz.correctExplanation: Denser join, smaller legal miss. Same classes of killer, new factory.
objectiveIds: Contrast a hybrid bond with a solder bump as a density and thermal choice

quiz.stem: Hybrid bonding versus solder bumps is a trade because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Hybrid buys pitch and a better thermal path, and spends cleanliness, die-to-die overlay, and known-good-die test

distractors.text: Hybrid bonds are lossless and ignore particles
distractors.rationale: A smaller pad is a pickier pad.

distractors.text: Solder automatically yields better than any model
distractors.rationale: Solder is forgiving and fat, not magic.

distractors.text: Either join repeals the wafer yield model
distractors.rationale: The dice still have to yield.

quiz.correctExplanation: Density versus forgiveness. That is the join's triangle.
objectiveIds: Contrast a hybrid bond with a solder bump as a density and thermal choice

lessons.title: One beam cannot visit every feature in time
explanation: In-line metrology already taught measuring before the lot is lost. At leading-edge CDs the number of features on a wafer outgrows a single electron or optical beam. Visiting every contact, every via, every line edge would take longer than the process step you are trying to control. Multi-beam write and inspection split the work across many columns so the visit finishes in factory time.

This is not a new physics of electrons. It is a throughput argument identical in shape to the EUV dose/WPH budget: events per second versus events demanded. Mask write has the same problem — a single beam cannot paint a High-NA, OPC-heavy reticle in a night. Inspection of stochastic leftovers has it worse, because the killers are sparse and small.
Read 'multi-beam' as: the metrology and mask shops hit the same wall the scanner hit. More columns, or you sample and hope. Sampling is how stochastic tails hide.
lessons.example: After-develop inspection with one beam samples 1% of contacts and calls the lot clean. Electrical test finds a motif-clustered missing-hole population the sample missed. A multi-beam inspect of the same layer sees the cluster in time to stop the next lot. The process did not change. The visit rate did.
lessons.whyItMatters: If inspection is 'a tool that looks', you will believe a clean sample. If it is a visit-rate budget, you will ask what fraction of the tail anyone actually saw.

quiz.stem: Multi-beam write and inspection exist because:
quiz.correctAnswer: A single beam cannot visit every leading-edge feature in factory time

distractors.text: Electrons stopped interacting with silicon
distractors.rationale: The physics still works. The clock does not.

distractors.text: k1 is the number of beams
distractors.rationale: k1 is lithography cleverness.

distractors.text: Overlay residuals are a form of electron beam
distractors.rationale: Placement is not a column count.

quiz.correctExplanation: Events demanded versus events per second. Split the work or miss the tail.
objectiveIds: Explain multi-beam write and inspection as what you do when a single beam cannot visit every feature in time

quiz.stem: A lot that looks clean on a 1% single-beam sample and fails electrical on one motif usually means:
quiz.correctAnswer: The visit rate missed a clustered tail; the process may have been screaming in the other 99%

distractors.text: Electrical test invented contacts that were never drawn
distractors.rationale: The motif was drawn. The sample missed it.

distractors.text: The Czochralski notch failed at probe
distractors.rationale: A notch is not this cluster.

distractors.text: Wet oxidation during inspect deleted the sample
distractors.rationale: No oxidant step ran in the SEM.

quiz.correctExplanation: Sparse killers plus a thin sample is how a tail hides. Multi-beam is how you thicken the sample.
objectiveIds: Predict why leading-edge CD and defect inspection outgrow a single-beam tool

quiz.stem: Sampling versus adding columns is a trade because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Sampling is cheap and hides sparse tails; more columns spend tool cost and see the killers in time

distractors.text: Sampling always sees every stochastic hole
distractors.rationale: That is what it does not do.

distractors.text: Columns automatically thicken depth of focus
distractors.rationale: Beams are not an NA knob.

distractors.text: Either choice repeals the yield model
distractors.rationale: Metrology feeds the model. It does not cancel it.

quiz.correctExplanation: Time versus coverage. The tail only exists if someone visits it.
objectiveIds: Predict why leading-edge CD and defect inspection outgrow a single-beam tool

lessons.title: A scanner is a factory. Depreciation shows up in the die.
explanation: A High-NA or even a 0.33-NA EUV scanner costs what a factory used to cost. Depreciation per hour, divided by wafers per hour, is a cost per wafer. Yield turns that into a cost per good die. A layer that prints but only at a dose that halves WPH just doubled its scanner bill. A layer that moves to High-NA and then needs two stitched fields pays twice on the scarce tool.

So cost per wafer is not an accountant's afterthought. It is throughput times yield times a machine you cannot buy two of this quarter. Multipatterned 193 can still win a layer on cost even when High-NA can print it, if the 193 tools exist and the EUV hours do not.
Read any 'we adopted High-NA' sentence with a cost question: which layers, at what dose, at what WPH, at what yield. Without those, it is a press release.
lessons.example: A via layer can be one High-NA pass at a stochastic dose that yields 40 WPH, or two 0.33 passes at 80 WPH each on a cheaper tool. The 'advanced' choice is the expensive one. The cost model, not the Rayleigh criterion, picks.
lessons.whyItMatters: If cost is rude to mention in a physics course, you will believe every layer should move to the newest cone. The factory will not.

quiz.stem: A scanner's depreciation shows up in the die because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Cost per wafer is hours of a scarce machine divided by WPH, then divided again by yield

distractors.text: Tools are free once the first wafer prints
distractors.rationale: The machine is still being paid for.

distractors.text: k1 is the depreciation schedule
distractors.rationale: k1 is process cleverness.

distractors.text: Yield cancels capital cost by definition
distractors.rationale: Yield turns wafer cost into die cost. It does not delete it.

quiz.correctExplanation: Time on the tool, times the tool, over good dice. That is the bill.
objectiveIds: Treat a scanner as a factory whose depreciation shows up in the die

quiz.stem: A High-NA layer that prints and still dominates wafer cost usually:
quiz.correctAnswer: Is sitting on a scarce tool at a dose or stitch count that wrecked WPH

distractors.text: Has repealed depreciation by printing at all
distractors.rationale: Printing is necessary, not sufficient.

distractors.text: Must be using 193 nm glass again
distractors.rationale: The expensive tool is the EUV family.

distractors.text: Has a k1 of zero so the tool is free
distractors.rationale: k1 is not a price.

quiz.correctExplanation: It printed. It printed slowly on the machine you cannot buy more of. That is dominance.
objectiveIds: Predict why a slower, higher-dose EUV layer can dominate wafer cost even if it prints

quiz.stem: Leaving a layer on multipatterned 193 instead of High-NA can be the cost winner when:
quiz.correctAnswer: The older tools exist, their hours are cheaper, and the EUV hours are the scarce resource

distractors.text: 193 nm always has better resolution than 0.55 NA at 13.5
distractors.rationale: This is a cost sentence, not a Rayleigh sentence.

distractors.text: High-NA tools have no depreciation
distractors.rationale: They have more of it.

distractors.text: Yield models ignore which tool ran the layer
distractors.rationale: WPH is tool-specific. So is the bill.

quiz.correctExplanation: Physics can print it on the new cone. The factory may not want to.
objectiveIds: Predict why a slower, higher-dose EUV layer can dominate wafer cost even if it prints

lessons.title: Cost, heat, stochastics, and a spent wavelength
explanation: This course's last sentence is not a new device. It is why the old sentence — shrink λ, raise NA, wrap the channel, ship a bigger die — no longer pays for itself. Wavelength already jumped to 13.5 nm. The next jump is not on the calendar the way 193-to-EUV was. NA can still move, and High-NA showed the bill: field, focus, photons, money. Stochastics do not care that the optic could print the pitch. Heat does not care that the CFET inverter is smaller. Cost does not care that the slide is pretty.

The wall is the product of those constraints, not the maximum of them. A layer can have the pitch and lose on count. A die can have the pitch and lose on e^(−A·D). A package can have the bandwidth and throttle. Another wrap or another cone can move one term and worsen two others.
Read a node announcement by naming which term they bought and which term they spent. If the announcement names only the purchase, it is a brochure. You now own the vocabulary to finish the sentence.
lessons.example: A slide says High-NA plus GAA plus backside power 'enables the next node.' Translate: they bought a pitch, a wrap, and some front-side tracks. They spent a stitch overlay, a release etch, a grind, a photon tail, and a depreciation line. Whether that is a node depends on those spends, not on the shopping list.
lessons.whyItMatters: The reporter who can name the spend will not confuse a platform announcement with cheap scaling. Cheap scaling already left, when λ jumped and the triangle closed.

quiz.stem: The scaling wall is cost, heat, stochastics, and a spent wavelength because:
quiz.correctAnswer: λ already jumped, NA and wraps still spend other budgets, and the product of those spends is the node

distractors.text: Physics forbids any further device or optic change
distractors.rationale: Changes still happen. They no longer come cheap.

distractors.text: k1 has been repealed by law
distractors.rationale: k1 still exists. It is not the wall.

distractors.text: Only heat remains; photons and money are free
distractors.rationale: The wall is the product of the terms.

quiz.correctExplanation: Four constraints, one product. That is why another cone is not a renaissance.
objectiveIds: Name the wall as cost, heat, stochastics, and the fact that wavelength already jumped

quiz.stem: A node slide that lists High-NA, GAA, and backside power and names no spend is usually:
quiz.correctAnswer: A shopping list; the node is whether stitch, release, grind, count, and depreciation still close

distractors.text: Proof that all five spends went to zero
distractors.rationale: Unnamed is not zero.

distractors.text: A reason to ignore the yield model
distractors.rationale: Area and D still fight.

distractors.text: A legal requirement to skip overlay
distractors.rationale: The stitch is still a pair.

quiz.correctExplanation: Purchases without spends are brochures. You can now name the spends.
objectiveIds: Predict why another NA or another device wrap does not automatically restore cheap scaling

quiz.stem: Another NA step or another wrap does not automatically restore cheap scaling because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Each buys one term and typically spends photons, field, heat, or depreciation the last purchase already strained

distractors.text: No further NA or wrap is physically imaginable
distractors.rationale: They are imaginable. They are not cheap.

distractors.text: Wavelength can jump every year for free
distractors.rationale: The last jump already happened.

distractors.text: Cost models ignore which tool and which film ran
distractors.rationale: Cost is exactly those choices.

quiz.correctExplanation: A purchase is not a renaissance. The wall is the spend you did not put on the slide.
objectiveIds: Predict why another NA or another device wrap does not automatically restore cheap scaling
